title: Scrotal Swelling - Hydrocele History
patient_instructions: You are a 25-year-old man who noticed a painless swelling on one side of your scrotum a few weeks to a couple of months ago, spotted incidentally in the shower. If asked: it is on the left side, has slowly grown, is NOT painful to touch, and does not change much with standing or lying down. You have NO redness, no penile discharge, no burning or increased frequency of urine, no fever/chills/flu-like illness, no facial swelling, no weight loss, no appetite change, and no lumps elsewhere or in the groin. You have not lost sensation over the scrotum. No trauma. No heavy lifting, chronic cough or constipation; no abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting. Sexual history: you are sexually active with a stable female partner, use condoms most of the time, no previous STIs, no multiple partners recently. Ideas: you are worried it could be cancer. Concerns: your fertility and your health. Expectations: you want to know what it is and what happens next. Affect: anxious, a bit embarrassed, relieved by a calm approach. If the candidate asks examination-type questions (consistency, whether you can get above it, transillumination) politely say those are things they would find on examining you.
candidate_instructions: You are the GP. A 25-year-old man presents with a painless scrotal swelling. Task: take a focused 6-minute history including a sensitive sexual history, then explain your provisional diagnosis and differentials to the patient. You should also briefly outline the key examination findings you would seek and first-line investigations.
examiner_instructions: Look for a structured swelling history (onset, course, laterality, pain, positional change) and a competent, sensitively-conducted sexual history. The candidate must actively screen for and mention testicular cancer (the not-to-miss diagnosis in a man aged 20-40) and must at least consider testicular torsion even though this is a painless chronic swelling (sudden severe pain, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex would point to torsion). The likely diagnosis is hydrocele; strong candidates cite the examination triad - confined to scrotum, able to 'get above' it, and transilluminates - and state that a secondary hydrocele in a young man mandates scrotal ultrasound to exclude an underlying tumour before reassurance. First-line investigation is scrotal ultrasound; tumour markers are AFP, beta-hCG and LDH. Prompt if needed: 'What is the single most important diagnosis you must not miss?'

criteria: Introduces self, acknowledges sensitivity, addresses the patient's anxiety
Explores the swelling: onset, course, laterality, pain, positional change (avoids asking examination findings)
Takes a structured, non-judgemental sexual history (activity, partners, protection, prior STI)
Screens trauma, hernia risk factors and viral orchitis (mumps) features
States hydrocele as the likely diagnosis with reasoning (painless, transilluminable, confined to scrotum)
Actively includes and screens testicular CANCER as the must-not-miss diagnosis in a man aged 20-40
Considers epididymo-orchitis, hernia, varicocele/spermatocele/haematocele and testicular torsion
States scrotal ultrasound as first-line investigation and orders tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG, LDH)
Recognises a secondary hydrocele mandates excluding an underlying testicular tumour before reassurance
Offers STI screen where relevant and appropriate management by cause (conservative, surgery if malignancy, treat STI)
Handles intimate/sexual history with confidentiality, tact and clear signposting
Explains diagnosis and next steps in reassuring, understandable lay terms

red_flags: Testicular cancer - a painless firm intratesticular lump with loss of testicular sensation, possible reactive hydrocele, in a man aged 20-40; must be excluded before diagnosing a simple hydrocele
Testicular torsion - sudden severe scrotal pain, high-riding testis and absent cremasteric reflex; a surgical emergency requiring exploration within ~6 hours
A secondary hydrocele in a young man (may overlie an underlying tumour) - always requires scrotal ultrasound
Strangulated/incarcerated inguinoscrotal hernia - swelling with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and irreducibility
australian_guidelines: Therapeutic Guidelines: if epididymo-orchitis is sexually acquired (younger men), treat empirically for Chlamydia/gonorrhoea (ceftriaxone 500 mg IM stat plus doxycycline 100 mg BD for 10-14 days) and arrange contact tracing; cover Gram-negatives if an enteric urinary source is likely in older men.
RACGP / Murtagh: any painless firm testicular lump in a young man must be investigated with scrotal ultrasound and tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG, LDH) to exclude germ-cell tumour before reassurance.
ASHM / Australian STI guidelines: offer a full STI screen (chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B) where a sexually acquired cause is possible.
learning_objectives: Take a focused history for scrotal swelling and distinguish history features from examination findings.
Conduct a sensitive, structured sexual history.
Always include and exclude testicular cancer and testicular torsion in any scrotal presentation.
Recognise the hydrocele examination triad and the need for ultrasound in a secondary hydrocele.
Outline first-line investigations and cause-directed management.
key_points: The hydrocele triad: swelling confined to the scrotum, able to 'get above' it (excludes inguinoscrotal hernia), and transilluminates.
Testicular cancer is the most common solid malignancy in men aged 20-40 and must always be excluded.
A secondary hydrocele in a young man requires scrotal ultrasound to exclude an underlying tumour.
Immediate swelling after trauma suggests a haematocele; delayed swelling suggests a hydrocele.
First-line investigation is scrotal ultrasound; tumour markers are AFP, beta-hCG and LDH.

citations.claim: A swelling confined to the scrotum must be differentiated from an inguinoscrotal hernia; most true scrotal swellings are benign but testicular tumours are the key not-to-miss diagnosis in men aged 20-40.
Hydrocele features: confined to scrotum, surrounds the testis (which becomes impalpable/non-tender), smooth pear-shaped, and transilluminates.

Acutely painful scrotal swellings mandate early diagnosis; causes include torsion of the testis, torsion of a testicular appendage, epididymo-orchitis, trauma/haematocele and strangulated inguinoscrotal hernia.
Testicular cancer typically presents in young men 20-40 as a painless firm lump with loss of testicular sensation and a possible reactive hydrocele.
